lead: Laser action turns a pumped gain medium into an oscillator. Three things must happen together: the pump must create population inversion so stimulated emission beats absorption; mirrors must feed light back through the medium; and the pump must be strong enough to cross a threshold where round-trip gain equals round-trip loss. Below threshold the device behaves like an LED. Above threshold it emits narrow-linewidth, coherent light. Fiber links use this for long-haul transmitters, where launch power and spectral width matter. This chapter gives the conditions; 3.4 builds the diode.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for stimulated emission, 3.2 for recombination, and Unit 1 for cavity modes.

blocks.text: At thermal equilibrium, N<sub>2</sub>/N<sub>1</sub> = exp[−(E<sub>2</sub>−E<sub>1</sub>)/(k<sub>B</sub>T)], where k<sub>B</sub> is the Boltzmann constant (1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K) and T is the absolute temperature in kelvin. The lower level N<sub>1</sub> is fuller, so absorption beats stimulated emission. A pump lifts atoms to an upper level. A metastable upper level holds them long enough for a photon to arrive. Population inversion means N<sub>2</sub> > N<sub>1</sub>. Then stimulated emission exceeds absorption and the medium has gain. A semiconductor uses carrier density and quasi-Fermi levels instead of two discrete levels, but the test is the same: pump the active region until stimulated emission beats absorption. Only a few universities teach the full derivation; exams ask the condition and the gain formula.

blocks.where: g is gain per unit length (cm⁻¹); σ is the stimulated-emission cross-section (cm²); N<sub>2</sub> and N<sub>1</sub> are populations per unit volume (cm⁻³). Both N values are densities, not total counts.

blocks.text: Gain alone gives a single-pass amplifier. A Fabry-Perot cavity puts two mirrors around the gain medium and sends light back and forth. At threshold, round-trip gain equals total loss. Above threshold gain clamps and extra pump becomes output. The cavity also selects longitudinal modes: 2nL = mλ, where n is refractive index, λ is vacuum wavelength and m is an integer. Mode spacing is Δν = c/(2n<sub>g</sub>L), with c the speed of light and n<sub>g</sub> the group index (n<sub>g</sub> ≈ n far from band edges). Threshold current is the pump current where the gain condition is first met. Threshold current density falls with lower α<sub>i</sub>, longer L, higher R<sub>1</sub>R<sub>2</sub>, or higher Γ. For a fixed stripe width the total threshold current still rises with L, because the pumped volume grows. This is why laser diodes confine light and carriers tightly.

blocks.where: Γ is the confinement factor (fraction of the mode in the gain medium); g<sub>th</sub> is threshold material gain (cm⁻¹); α<sub>i</sub> is internal loss (cm⁻¹); L is cavity length (cm); R<sub>1</sub> and R<sub>2</sub> are mirror power reflectances (dimensionless).

figure.caption: Pump raises the medium into inversion; the gain medium and mirrors form a feedback loop, and a partial mirror lets light out. Notice that without the feedback edge there is no oscillator.

spec.aria: Block diagram of a laser: pump creates inversion, the gain medium is fed back by mirrors, and output leaves through a partial mirror.

examples.question: A Fabry-Perot semiconductor laser has L = 300 μm, R1 = R2 = 0.32, internal loss α_i = 10 cm⁻¹ and confinement factor Γ = 0.30. Find the threshold modal gain and threshold material gain.
steps: Threshold modal gain Γg_th = α_i + mirror loss = 10 + 37.98 = 47.98 cm⁻¹.
examples.answer: Threshold modal gain is 47.98 cm⁻¹ and threshold material gain is 159.94 cm⁻¹.
examples.check:
import math
L_um = 300.0
L_cm = L_um * 1e-4
R1 = 0.32
R2 = 0.32
alpha_i = 10.0
Gamma = 0.30
mirror_loss = (1.0/(2.0*L_cm)) * math.log(1.0/(R1*R2))
modal_gain = alpha_i + mirror_loss
material_gain = modal_gain / Gamma
print(f"{modal_gain:.2f}")
print(f"{material_gain:.2f}")

traps: Mixing centimetres and metres in 1/(2L): convert L to the unit of α_i first. In the example, 300 μm = 0.03 cm.
Forgetting Γ: the threshold condition limits modal gain Γg_th, so material gain is g_th = Γg_th/Γ.
Using R instead of R1R2: mirror loss needs the product, not one mirror.
Calling any strong pump inversion: inversion requires N2 > N1, not merely a large N2.
Saying gain grows without limit above threshold: gain clamps near threshold and extra pump becomes output.

quiz.q: State the condition for population inversion.
quiz.a: N₂ > N₁; more atoms sit in the upper laser level than the lower.
It returns photons through the gain medium so one pass adds gain repeatedly; without it, the device is only an amplifier.

quiz.q: A cavity has L = 0.05 cm, α_i = 5 cm⁻¹, R₁ = R₂ = 0.30, Γ = 0.20. Find Γg_th.
Why does threshold current fall when Γ rises?
quiz.a: Higher Γ means more of the mode overlaps the gain region, so a smaller material gain reaches the same modal gain; less pump current is needed.

quiz.q: What selects longitudinal modes in a Fabry-Perot cavity?
quiz.a: The round-trip phase condition 2nL = mλ; only wavelengths satisfying it resonate.

quiz.q: A laser has threshold current 20 mA at 25°C. Assume, for practice, that it rises 1.5% per °C. Estimate it at 35°C.
quiz.a: Factor = 1.015¹⁰ = 1.1605; I_th = 20 × 1.1605 = 23.21 mA. The 1.5% per °C is an assumed figure for practice; real InGaAsP diodes are far more temperature sensitive, and threshold roughly doubles over a few tens of degrees.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real transmitters use distributed feedback or distributed Bragg reflector gratings to pick one longitudinal mode; vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers use tiny cavities and high-reflectance mirrors. Quantum-well and quantum-dot active regions lower threshold current. Researchers study gain switching and mode locking for short pulses. Search: DFB laser threshold, VCSEL, longitudinal mode spacing.
